qs.q: A 10-year-old patient with a repaired myelomeningocele presents with progressive scoliosis, worsening lower extremity spasticity, and a declining sensory level. Magnetic resonance imaging confirms that the spinal cord is anchored abnormally low. What pathophysiological mechanism explains these secondary deficits?
o: Traction and ischemia of the spinal cord during growth
Direct bacterial colonization from an unsealed dermal sinus
Cerebrospinal fluid hypersecretion from the choroid plexus
Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct by cerebellar vermis descent
qs.e: A tethered cord is anchored low and gets stretched or traumatized during somatic growth, producing progressive neurological deficits, pain, and skeletal deformities like scoliosis. Aqueduct obstruction leads to hydrocephalus rather than isolated spinal cord traction symptoms.
qs.s: Spina Bifida and Neural Tube Defects: Meningocele and Myelomeningocele: MCQs

es.q: An 80-year-old bedridden patient with severe scoliosis experiences sudden respiratory distress. Explain the difference in mechanism and reversibility between 'resorption atelectasis' and 'contraction atelectasis'.
es.m: Resorption atelectasis occurs when an obstruction (e.g., mucous plug, foreign body, tumor, or asthma) prevents air from entering distal airways, causing the existing air to be absorbed and the lung volume to decrease. This type is potentially reversible. Contraction atelectasis is caused by local or generalized fibrosis within the lung or pleura that prevents full lung expansion and increases elastic recoil. This type of atelectasis is irreversible.

ai.clinicalScope: Adolescent idiopathic and secondary scoliosis in children and adolescents presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.title: Scoliosis in Children and Adolescents
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Scoliosis is a three‑dimensional spinal curvature >10° on standing radiograph. In low‑resource settings it is often discovered incidentally or when deformity progresses, and may be idiopathic or secondary to neurofibromatosis, infection or trauma.

sections.p: A structural lateral curvature of the spine with rotation, measured by the Cobb angle on a standing AP radiograph.
b: Cobb angle ≥10° confirms scoliosis
Rotation evident on the rib hump or vertebral pedicle asymmetry
Standing posture required for accurate measurement
Mild: Cobb 10‑24°, observe with serial exams
Moderate: Cobb 25‑44°, consider bracing
Severe: Cobb ≥45°, surgical referral
Progression risk highest during growth spurt (Risser 0‑2)

sections.p: In East Africa the majority are idiopathic; secondary causes must be sought when red flags appear.
b: Idiopathic (≈80% of cases, peak 10‑16 y)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) – café‑au‑lait spots, neurofibromas
Congenital vertebral anomalies (hemivertebrae)
Post‑infectious (spinal TB, pyogenic spondylitis)
Traumatic vertebral fracture

sections.p: Patients or caregivers notice asymmetry; physical exam confirms.
b: Shoulder height difference, scapular prominence
Waist asymmetry, trunk shift
Rib hump on forward bend (Adam’s test)
Occasional back pain or leg length discrepancy
Neurologic symptoms only if severe rotation or associated lesion

sections.p: Imaging confirms curvature, assesses etiology and progression.

t.b: Measures Cobb angle and rotation; defines severity
Detects intraspinal lesions (tumour, syrinx, TB abscess); essential when neurologic signs present

t.a: Ultrasound of the abdomen (if leg length discrepancy)
t.b: Rules out pelvic or renal causes of asymmetry

t.a: Genetic testing for NF1 (clinical criteria often sufficient)
t.b: Confirms NF1 when skin findings equivocal

t.a: If MRI unavailable, refer for CT or clinical monitoring
t.b: CT can show bony anomalies; if not possible, base decisions on X‑ray and exam

b: Rapid progression >5° in 3 months during growth spurt
Neurologic deficit (weakness, sensory loss, bladder/bowel changes)
Severe thoracic curve >70° risking cardiopulmonary compromise
Associated NF1 lesions causing pain or functional loss
Signs of spinal infection (fever, night pain, weight loss)

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, then halt progression and correct deformity.
b: Idiopathic mild: observation every 6 months, physiotherapy for core strength
Moderate curves in growing child: thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO) worn ≥18 h/day; monitor Cobb every 4‑6 months
Severe or progressive despite bracing: refer for posterior spinal fusion (if surgical services exist)
NF1‑related scoliosis: earlier surgical referral, avoid aggressive bracing if vertebral dysplasia present
Infection‑related scoliosis: anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) for 6‑9 months, then orthopaedic correction
Clinic review every 6 months until skeletal maturity (Risser 5)
Repeat standing X‑ray if growth spurt ongoing or brace compliance doubtful
Educate families on brace wear, posture, and activity modification
Screen NF1 patients yearly for new spinal curves
Encourage nutrition and vitamin D to support bone health

sections.p: Distinguish scoliosis from other spinal deformities.
b: Kyphosis – sagittal hyper‑lordosis without lateral curvature; thoracic hump on lateral view
Pott disease (spinal TB) – vertebral collapse, gibbus, systemic symptoms; MRI shows abscess
Congenital scoliosis – fixed structural anomaly present at birth, often hemivertebrae
Mild Cobb angles may be under‑estimated on poor‑quality films; repeat if doubt
Absence of neurologic signs does not exclude intraspinal tumour; MRI still indicated if rapid progression
Normal X‑ray does not rule out early vertebral infection; consider ESR/CRP and clinical picture

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset back pain with fever
New weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel dysfunction
Severe thoracic curve >70° causing breathing difficulty

faq.q: What is the minimum Cobb angle to call a curve scoliosis?
faq.a: A Cobb angle of 10° or more on a standing AP radiograph.

faq.q: Why is bracing less effective after skeletal maturity?
faq.a: Growth plates have closed, so the spine no longer remodels; curves become fixed.
Physiotherapy improves muscle balance but does not halt progression of moderate‑to‑severe curves without a brace.
